Title: What business problem must getBill solve first?
Why it matters: It sets the priority for every later decision.
Examples of possible answers: Bill customers accurately each month. Show each team what it spends. Cut cloud waste.

Title: How will you measure whether getBill is successful?
Why it matters: A measurable target shows whether the work paid off.
Examples of possible answers: Every bill issued by the third business day. Fewer billing disputes. Cloud spend reduced by 10%.

Title: Is getBill for FPT's own cloud costs, for customers' costs, or for both?
Why it matters: Rebilling customers and managing internal costs have different rules and different users.
Examples of possible answers: FPT's own costs. Customers' costs. Both.

Title: Which capabilities must the first release include?
Why it matters: It decides the scope of the first release.
Examples of possible answers: Billing and invoicing only. Billing plus dashboards and budgets. Full FinOps, including savings recommendations.

Title: Which capabilities can wait for later releases?
Why it matters: It keeps the first release small enough to deliver.
Examples of possible answers: Forecasting. Savings recommendations. Carbon reporting.

Title: Is there a date by which the first release must be in use?
Why it matters: A date decides what can fit in the first release.
Examples of possible answers: A date tied to a customer contract. The start of the fiscal year. No fixed date.

Title: Who makes the final decision when two requirements conflict?
Why it matters: Someone must settle trade-offs quickly.
Examples of possible answers: The product owner. A steering group. The head of finance.

Title: Will getBill be offered to other companies, or used only by FPT and its customers?
Why it matters: Offering it to other companies adds licensing, support and stricter separation of data.
Examples of possible answers: FPT and its customers only. Offered to other companies later. Not decided.

Title: Which existing tools must getBill replace, and which must it work alongside?
Why it matters: Overlap with other tools wastes money and confuses users.
Examples of possible answers: Replaces the Excel workbooks. Works alongside AWS Cost Explorer. Replaces a commercial FinOps tool.

Title: What budget is there to build getBill?
Why it matters: The budget limits the scope and the size of the team.
Examples of possible answers: A fixed amount for the first year. Funded one release at a time.

Title: What budget is there to run getBill each month?
Why it matters: Cloud storage, queries and dashboards cost money every month.
Examples of possible answers: A fixed monthly limit. A share of the cloud spend it manages. Charged to customers.

Title: Which groups of people will use getBill?
Why it matters: Each group needs its own views and permissions.
Examples of possible answers: The FinOps team. Finance. Engineering teams. Executives. Account managers. Customers.

Title: Roughly how many people in each group will use getBill?
Why it matters: The number of users decides licensing costs and portal capacity.
Examples of possible answers: Five FinOps staff. Fifty engineers. Two hundred customer users.

Title: Is there a FinOps team today, and who is on it?
Why it matters: A FinOps team usually owns getBill's rules and reviews.
Examples of possible answers: A dedicated team. Part of the cloud team. No team yet.

Title: Who is responsible for cloud costs in each business unit or customer?
Why it matters: Reports and alerts need a named person who can act on them.
Examples of possible answers: Each engineering manager. Each customer's finance contact. A central team.

Title: Which groups may change data or settings, and which may only view?
Why it matters: It defines the roles and permissions in getBill.
Examples of possible answers: Finance approves bills. Engineers only view. Account managers change pricing rules.

Title: How technical are the main users?
Why it matters: It decides how much must work without writing queries.
Examples of possible answers: Mostly finance staff who use Excel. Engineers who write SQL. A mix.

Title: Which languages must the screens and reports support?
Why it matters: Users may need their own language.
Examples of possible answers: English. Vietnamese. Both.

Title: Do customers' own staff need to sign in to getBill?
Why it matters: Customer access needs a customer portal and strict separation of each customer's data.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, for every customer. Only for some customers. No, they only receive files.

Title: Which sign-in system must FPT staff use?
Why it matters: Staff should sign in with the accounts they already have.
Examples of possible answers: Microsoft Entra ID. Okta. AWS IAM Identity Center.

Title: Which sign-in system must customers use?
Why it matters: Customers may want to use their own organization's accounts.
Examples of possible answers: Each customer's own identity provider. Accounts that getBill creates.

Title: Must customers be able to manage their own users, or does a central administrator do it?
Why it matters: Letting customers manage their users saves FPT staff time.
Examples of possible answers: A central administrator only. Each customer manages its own users.

Title: What training or help must users get?
Why it matters: Users who do not understand the numbers stop using the tool.
Examples of possible answers: Written guides. Short videos. Training sessions. Explanations inside the screens.

Title: Which clouds hold the costs that getBill must cover now?
Why it matters: Each cloud needs its own connection.
Examples of possible answers: AWS. Microsoft Azure. Google Cloud. Oracle Cloud.

Title: Which clouds will be added in the next two years?
Why it matters: Planning for them now avoids a redesign later.
Examples of possible answers: Google Cloud. Oracle Cloud. None.

Title: For each customer and each cloud, who owns the billing account: FPT or the customer?
Why it matters: The owner sets up the billing export and approves access to it.
Examples of possible answers: FPT owns all of them. Each customer owns its own. It differs by customer and by cloud.

Title: How many AWS organizations, Azure billing accounts and Google Cloud billing accounts are there?
Why it matters: Each one needs its own connection and permissions.
Examples of possible answers: One AWS organization. Ten customer AWS organizations. Three Azure billing accounts.

Title: Which Microsoft agreement does each Azure billing account use?
Why it matters: Each agreement type offers different billing exports and permissions.
Examples of possible answers: Enterprise Agreement. Microsoft Customer Agreement. Cloud Solution Provider. Pay-as-you-go.

Title: Through which AWS partner program does FPT resell AWS?
Why it matters: The program decides which billing data, discounts and tools FPT receives from AWS.
Examples of possible answers: The AWS Solution Provider Program. Through an AWS distributor. Both.

Title: May getBill read billing data directly from a customer's cloud account?
Why it matters: Direct access needs the customer's approval and a trust relationship between the accounts.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, through a read-only role. No, the customer must send files. Each customer chooses.

Title: Who at each customer approves giving getBill access to its billing data?
Why it matters: Access stalls without a named approver.
Examples of possible answers: The customer's cloud administrator. Its security team. Its finance lead.

Title: May getBill store long-lived keys or passwords to reach a billing source?
Why it matters: Stored keys must be rotated and can leak.
Examples of possible answers: No, short-lived access only. Yes, if rotated every 90 days. Only for SaaS vendors.

Title: How quickly must getBill's access be removed when a customer leaves?
Why it matters: Access that is left in place is a security risk.
Examples of possible answers: The same day. Within a week. At the end of the contract.

Title: Does FPT also resell Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud?
Why it matters: Reselling another cloud adds that provider's partner billing data and rules.
Examples of possible answers: Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider. Google Cloud partner reselling. AWS only.

Title: Does FPT use AWS Billing Conductor today?
Why it matters: AWS Billing Conductor already applies a reseller's own prices, so getBill may use it or replace it.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, for every customer. For some customers. No.

Title: May resold customers use AWS's own cost tools, such as AWS Cost Explorer, in their accounts?
Why it matters: Customers who see AWS's prices in those tools can find different numbers from FPT's bill.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, showing FPT's prices. Yes, showing AWS's public prices. No access.

Title: Which billing data must getBill read from each cloud?
Why it matters: Each export has a different level of detail.
Examples of possible answers: AWS Cost and Usage Report 2.0. The AWS export in the FOCUS format. Azure Cost Management exports. Google Cloud's billing export to BigQuery.

Title: Must getBill store all cost data in FOCUS, the common billing format of the FinOps Foundation?
Why it matters: A common format makes costs from different clouds comparable.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, FOCUS for everything. FOCUS plus each cloud's own detail. No preference.

Title: How many months of past cost data must getBill load when it starts?
Why it matters: Trends and forecasts need history.
Examples of possible answers: Three months. Thirteen months. Three years.

Title: How up to date must the cost data be?
Why it matters: Fresher data costs more to process.
Examples of possible answers: Updated daily. Updated several times a day. Monthly is enough.

Title: Do you need costs by the hour, by the day or by the month?
Why it matters: Hourly data is much larger, but it shows usage patterns.
Examples of possible answers: By the hour. By the day. By the month.

Title: Must getBill show the cost of each individual resource, such as each server or storage bucket?
Why it matters: Resource detail makes the data much larger, but it shows exactly what costs money.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, always. Only for savings work. No, totals are enough.

Title: Must getBill include purchases made through cloud marketplaces?
Why it matters: Marketplace purchases appear on the cloud bill but belong to other vendors.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No. Only for some customers.

Title: Must getBill include costs from SaaS vendors?
Why it matters: SaaS bills arrive in different forms and need their own readers.
Examples of possible answers: Microsoft 365. Datadog. Snowflake. None.

Title: Must getBill include costs from data centers, private clouds or software licenses outside the cloud?
Why it matters: The total cost of technology needs every source.
Examples of possible answers: On-premises servers. VMware. Oracle licenses. No.

Title: Must getBill split the costs of shared Kubernetes clusters by team or application?
Why it matters: Shared clusters hide who uses what.
Examples of possible answers: Amazon EKS. Azure Kubernetes Service. Google Kubernetes Engine. No containers.

Title: Must getBill read the providers' list prices and FPT's negotiated prices?
Why it matters: Prices are needed to show discounts and estimate savings.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, both. List prices only. No.

Title: Who is the contact when a provider's billing data is late or wrong?
Why it matters: Someone must chase the provider or the customer.
Examples of possible answers: The cloud team. The customer's administrator. FPT's account manager.

Title: How should costs be grouped in reports?
Why it matters: The grouping becomes the structure of every report.
Examples of possible answers: By customer, then project. By business unit, cost center and application. By environment.

Title: How is each customer's or team's usage identified in each cloud?
Why it matters: getBill must know which costs belong to whom.
Examples of possible answers: Whole accounts, subscriptions or projects. Tags or labels on resources. A mix of both.

Title: Is there a tagging policy today, and which tags does it require?
Why it matters: Assigning costs by tags only works when the tags are applied.
Examples of possible answers: Owner, cost center and environment are required. No policy yet.

Title: What share of costs is tagged correctly today?
Why it matters: Poor tagging means much of the cost cannot be assigned.
Examples of possible answers: More than 90%. About half. Unknown.

Title: What should happen to costs that cannot be assigned to anyone?
Why it matters: Costs that belong to nobody must still appear somewhere.
Examples of possible answers: Show them as unassigned. Spread them in proportion to spend. Charge them to a central budget.

Title: May getBill assign costs with its own rules when tags are missing?
Why it matters: Rules can assign costs without changing the cloud resources.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, by account name. Yes, by a mapping table. No.

Title: How should shared costs, such as support plans, networking and security tools, be divided?
Why it matters: Each shared cost needs a rule for dividing it.
Examples of possible answers: In proportion to spend. Evenly. By fixed percentages. Not divided.

Title: How should commitment discounts, such as Savings Plans and reservations, be assigned?
Why it matters: The choice changes each team's or customer's cost.
Examples of possible answers: To the accounts that used them. To the account that bought them. Kept centrally.

Title: How should credits and refunds be assigned?
Why it matters: Credits can be large, and passing them on is a business decision.
Examples of possible answers: To the account that earned them. Kept by FPT. Shared across all customers.

Title: How should tax be shown?
Why it matters: Tax rules differ by country and by customer.
Examples of possible answers: As a separate line. Included in each line. Not shown.

Title: How often may the allocation rules change?
Why it matters: Frequent changes make month-to-month comparisons harder.
Examples of possible answers: Monthly. Quarterly. Rarely.

Title: When an allocation rule changes, should past months be recalculated?
Why it matters: Recalculating changes reports that people have already used.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, always. No, only future months. Only with approval.

Title: Who approves changes to allocation rules?
Why it matters: A rule change moves money between teams or customers.
Examples of possible answers: Finance. The FinOps team. Each customer.

Title: Must getBill produce customer invoices, internal chargeback, or reports for information only?
Why it matters: An invoice is a legal document, and a report for information only is not.
Examples of possible answers: Customer invoices. Internal chargeback. Information only. Several of these.

Title: Is getBill's bill the official invoice, or does an accounting system issue the invoice?
Why it matters: An accounting system needs the data in its own format.
Examples of possible answers: getBill issues the invoice. SAP issues it. QuickBooks issues it.

Title: Which kinds of pricing rules apply to customers?
Why it matters: Pricing rules decide what each customer pays.
Examples of possible answers: A markup percentage. A discount. A fixed monthly fee. Different rates for each service.

Title: Do customers receive the discounts that FPT gets from the providers?
Why it matters: Passing discounts on is a business decision that changes FPT's margin.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, all of them. Part of them. No.

Title: Who may change a customer's pricing rules?
Why it matters: A pricing change affects revenue.
Examples of possible answers: Account managers. Finance. The product owner.

Title: Must every pricing change be approved before it takes effect?
Why it matters: Approval stops mistakes before they reach an invoice.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, by finance. Only above a set amount. No.

Title: When a price changes partway through a month, which rate applies to which days?
Why it matters: Two rates in one month need a clear rule.
Examples of possible answers: The new rate from the day of the change. The new rate from the next month.

Title: How often is each customer billed?
Why it matters: It sets the billing schedule.
Examples of possible answers: Monthly. Quarterly. It differs by customer.

Title: By which day must each bill be issued?
Why it matters: The deadline sets the processing schedule.
Examples of possible answers: The fifth business day. The tenth day of the month.

Title: Must someone approve each bill before it is sent?
Why it matters: Approval catches errors before customers see them.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, finance approves every bill. Only bills above a set amount. No.

Title: In which currency must bills be issued?
Why it matters: Customers may need their local currency.
Examples of possible answers: US dollars. Vietnamese dong. The customer's choice.

Title: Where do exchange rates come from, and which day's rate is used?
Why it matters: The rate changes the amount owed.
Examples of possible answers: The bank's month-end rate. The provider's rate. A fixed rate each quarter.

Title: Do any providers bill in a currency other than US dollars?
Why it matters: Totals in different currencies must be converted before they can be added.
Examples of possible answers: All in US dollars. Azure bills some customers in local currency.

Title: What must each bill show?
Why it matters: The content decides how customers can check the bill.
Examples of possible answers: Totals by service. Totals by account. Every line item. A comparison with last month.

Title: How must amounts on a bill be rounded?
Why it matters: Rounding each line or only the total changes the amount owed.
Examples of possible answers: Round only the total. Round each line to two decimal places.

Title: How are billing disputes raised and handled?
Why it matters: Disputes need an owner and a process.
Examples of possible answers: Through the account manager. Through a support ticket. By email to finance.

Title: How is a correction issued after a bill was sent?
Why it matters: A wrong bill must be replaced in a way that can be traced.
Examples of possible answers: A credit note. A corrected bill. An adjustment on the next month's bill.

Title: Must getBill track whether customers have paid?
Why it matters: Payment tracking belongs to accounting unless getBill must do it.
Examples of possible answers: No, the accounting system tracks it. Yes, show paid and unpaid bills.

Title: Which discounts and credits does FPT receive from AWS as a reseller?
Why it matters: These discounts set FPT's margin on each customer.
Examples of possible answers: A partner discount on all usage. Discounts on certain services. Program credits.

Title: Should customers' bills start from AWS public prices or from FPT's own cost?
Why it matters: Starting from public prices keeps FPT's discount private, and starting from cost shows it.
Examples of possible answers: Public prices minus a customer discount. FPT's cost plus a markup. It differs by customer.

Title: How should AWS Support be charged to resold customers?
Why it matters: A reseller can provide support itself or pass on AWS's support charge.
Examples of possible answers: FPT's own support fee. AWS's support charge passed on. Included in the markup.

Title: Which taxes does FPT charge customers on resold AWS usage?
Why it matters: Resale adds taxes that do not appear on AWS's own bill.
Examples of possible answers: Vietnam value-added tax. U.S. sales tax. It depends on the customer's country.

Title: Do resold customers have a minimum monthly spend or a fixed contract term?
Why it matters: A customer who spends less than the minimum must be charged the difference.
Examples of possible answers: A monthly minimum. A yearly commitment. Neither.

Title: Which questions must the reports answer for each group of users?
Why it matters: Reports should answer real questions, not just show data.
Examples of possible answers: What did each customer spend? Which services grew? Where is money wasted?

Title: Which measures of cost must reports show?
Why it matters: Each measure gives a different total.
Examples of possible answers: Billed cost. Amortized cost. Cost after discounts. List price.

Title: Which key performance indicators must getBill track?
Why it matters: Indicators show whether cloud spending is under control.
Examples of possible answers: Cost per customer. Share of costs tagged. Commitment coverage. Forecast accuracy.

Title: Which dashboards does each group need?
Why it matters: Each dashboard needs its own data and access rules.
Examples of possible answers: An executive summary. A customer view. A view for each engineering team.

Title: How far back must users be able to compare costs?
Why it matters: Long comparisons need a long history.
Examples of possible answers: The last month. The last 13 months. Three years.

Title: Must users be able to go from totals down to individual resources?
Why it matters: Going down to resources needs detailed data and fast queries.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, to each resource. Only to each service. No.

Title: Must analysts be able to write their own queries on the data?
Why it matters: Self-service queries reduce requests to the engineering team.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, with SQL. Yes, with a report builder. No.

Title: Must users be able to export report data?
Why it matters: Exports let users work in their own tools.
Examples of possible answers: To Excel. To CSV. To PDF. No exports.

Title: Must some reports be sent automatically on a schedule?
Why it matters: Scheduled reports reach people who never sign in.
Examples of possible answers: Weekly by email. Monthly with the bill. No.

Title: Which reporting tool should users see?
Why it matters: The tool decides licensing costs and how reports are built.
Examples of possible answers: Amazon Quick Sight. Microsoft Power BI. A getBill web portal. No preference.

Title: How quickly must a dashboard open?
Why it matters: Slow dashboards drive users away.
Examples of possible answers: In under five seconds. In under thirty seconds.

Title: Must reports show exactly the same numbers as each provider's own cost tools?
Why it matters: Differences from the provider's tools cause doubt.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, exactly. Small differences are acceptable if they are explained.

Title: How should each group receive its bills and reports?
Why it matters: Many recipients cannot use cloud storage directly.
Examples of possible answers: A web portal. An email attachment. A file in the customer's own storage. SFTP.

Title: Which file formats must be delivered?
Why it matters: Each format needs its own builder.
Examples of possible answers: PDF. Excel. CSV. Parquet.

Title: Who must receive a copy of each bill besides the customer?
Why it matters: Finance and account managers may need copies.
Examples of possible answers: FPT finance. The account manager. Nobody.

Title: Should recipients be told when a bill or report is ready?
Why it matters: Without a notice, people use old results.
Examples of possible answers: An email. A Microsoft Teams message. No notice.

Title: May results be delivered into a customer's own cloud account?
Why it matters: Delivery outside FPT needs the customer's permission and a trust relationship.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, into the customer's storage. No, only through the portal or by email.

Title: Who must approve sending billing data outside FPT?
Why it matters: Sending data to the wrong place is a serious incident.
Examples of possible answers: The data owner. Security. Legal.

Title: What is the largest file a recipient can receive?
Why it matters: Email systems often refuse attachments over about 25 MB.
Examples of possible answers: 10 MB. 25 MB. No limit, because a download link is sent.

Title: How are lists of recipients kept up to date when people change jobs?
Why it matters: Bills sent to former staff leak data.
Examples of possible answers: The customer updates them in the portal. The account manager updates them.

Title: What counts as unusual spending?
Why it matters: Without a clear definition, alerts are either missed or too frequent.
Examples of possible answers: A daily rise of more than 30%. A new service appearing. Spending over a fixed amount.

Title: Should getBill find unusual spending with fixed limits or with statistical models?
Why it matters: Statistical models learn normal patterns, but their alerts are harder to explain.
Examples of possible answers: Fixed limits. Statistical models. Both.

Title: Who must be told about unusual spending?
Why it matters: An alert must reach someone who can act.
Examples of possible answers: The account owner. The FinOps team. The customer.

Title: How quickly must someone be told after unusual spending starts?
Why it matters: Every hour of a runaway cost adds to the bill.
Examples of possible answers: Within hours. By the next day. Weekly.

Title: Through which channel must these alerts arrive?
Why it matters: People ignore alerts in channels they do not watch.
Examples of possible answers: Email. Microsoft Teams. Slack. A ticket in ServiceNow or Jira.

Title: Must people record the cause of unusual spending and what they did about it?
Why it matters: A record shows patterns and proves that action was taken.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, in getBill. Yes, in the ticket system. No.

Title: How many false alarms are acceptable?
Why it matters: Too many false alarms make people ignore every alert.
Examples of possible answers: A few each month. None.

Title: At which levels must budgets be set?
Why it matters: Each level needs its own owner and alerts.
Examples of possible answers: For each customer. For each business unit. For each project. For each account.

Title: Who sets each budget?
Why it matters: Budgets without owners are ignored.
Examples of possible answers: Finance. Each team lead. Each customer.

Title: Should budgets cover a month, a quarter or a year?
Why it matters: The period decides how alerts are calculated.
Examples of possible answers: Monthly. Quarterly. Yearly, with monthly targets.

Title: When should a budget alert be sent?
Why it matters: Early alerts leave time to act.
Examples of possible answers: At 80% of the budget. At 100%. When the forecast passes the budget.

Title: Who must receive budget alerts?
Why it matters: Alerts must reach someone who can act.
Examples of possible answers: The budget owner. Finance. The customer.

Title: How far ahead must getBill forecast costs?
Why it matters: Longer forecasts are less accurate.
Examples of possible answers: To the end of the month. To the end of the quarter. Twelve months.

Title: How accurate must forecasts be?
Why it matters: An accuracy target shows whether forecasts can be trusted.
Examples of possible answers: Within 5%. Within 10%. No target.

Title: Should forecasts include planned changes, such as new projects or migrations?
Why it matters: Forecasts based only on history miss planned growth.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, entered by each team. No, history only.

Title: Must getBill compare each forecast with the actual spending afterwards?
Why it matters: The comparison improves later forecasts.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, every month. No.

Title: Must budgets be read from, or sent to, a financial planning system?
Why it matters: Budgets entered in two places drift apart.
Examples of possible answers: Read from Anaplan. Read from Excel. No other system.

Title: Which business measures should cloud cost be compared with?
Why it matters: Cost per unit shows whether spending grows faster than the business.
Examples of possible answers: Cost per customer. Cost per transaction. Cost per active user.

Title: Where do those business measures come from?
Why it matters: getBill must read them from somewhere.
Examples of possible answers: A product database. A finance system. Entered by hand.

Title: Who uses cost per unit, and for which decisions?
Why it matters: The use decides how detailed the figures must be.
Examples of possible answers: Executives, for pricing. Engineers, for design choices.

Title: Must getBill compare costs with targets or industry benchmarks?
Why it matters: Targets show whether a figure is good or bad.
Examples of possible answers: Internal targets. Industry benchmarks. No.

Title: Must getBill show FPT's margin on each customer's cloud resale?
Why it matters: The margin shows which customers are profitable.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, for FPT staff only. No.

Title: Which commitment discounts are used today?
Why it matters: getBill must track each kind.
Examples of possible answers: AWS Savings Plans. Reserved Instances. Azure reservations. Google Cloud committed use discounts.

Title: Who decides when to buy commitments?
Why it matters: Buying a commitment is a financial decision that lasts one to three years.
Examples of possible answers: The FinOps team. Finance. Each customer.

Title: Must getBill recommend which commitments to buy?
Why it matters: Recommendations need usage history and price data.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No, the providers' own recommendations are enough.

Title: Must getBill track how much of each commitment is used?
Why it matters: An unused commitment is money spent for nothing.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, daily. Yes, monthly. No.

Title: Which targets apply to commitment coverage and use?
Why it matters: Targets show whether commitments are well managed.
Examples of possible answers: 80% coverage and 95% use. No targets.

Title: Does FPT have negotiated spending agreements with any provider?
Why it matters: getBill must track progress against these agreements.
Examples of possible answers: An AWS private pricing agreement. A Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment. None.

Title: Must getBill track spending against these agreements?
Why it matters: Falling short of an agreed amount costs money.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No.

Title: Who receives the savings from commitments bought for customers?
Why it matters: The savings change each customer's price and FPT's margin.
Examples of possible answers: The customer. FPT. Shared between them.

Title: Must getBill show savings from spot capacity and other discounted capacity?
Why it matters: These savings show the value of engineering choices.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No.

Title: Should commitment discounts be shared across different customers in the same AWS organization?
Why it matters: AWS shares Savings Plans and Reserved Instances across all accounts in an organization unless sharing is turned off.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, FPT shares them and keeps the savings. No, each customer's discounts stay with that customer.

Title: Must getBill find idle or unused resources?
Why it matters: Idle resources are the easiest savings.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No.

Title: Must getBill recommend smaller or cheaper resource sizes?
Why it matters: Choosing the right size is a large source of savings.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No, the providers' own tools are enough.

Title: Which kinds of resources must be checked for savings?
Why it matters: Each kind needs its own checks.
Examples of possible answers: Servers. Databases. Storage. Kubernetes.

Title: Who acts on savings recommendations?
Why it matters: Recommendations without an owner are ignored.
Examples of possible answers: Each engineering team. The FinOps team. The customer.

Title: May getBill change resources automatically, such as stopping idle servers?
Why it matters: Automatic changes save money but can cause outages.
Examples of possible answers: No, recommendations only. Yes, in test environments only. Yes, with approval.

Title: Must getBill track the savings that were actually achieved?
Why it matters: Tracking proves the value of the FinOps work.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, for each team. Yes, for each customer. No.

Title: How should savings recommendations reach the people who act on them?
Why it matters: People act on work that appears in their own tools.
Examples of possible answers: A dashboard. A ticket in Jira or ServiceNow. A weekly email.

Title: Must getBill estimate the cost of a planned workload before it is built?
Why it matters: Estimates help teams choose cheaper designs.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No.

Title: Which software licenses run on cloud resources?
Why it matters: License costs can be larger than the server cost.
Examples of possible answers: Windows Server. SQL Server. Oracle. Red Hat.

Title: Are any licenses brought from your own agreements instead of bought through the cloud?
Why it matters: Your own licenses must be tracked against your contracts.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, Microsoft licenses. No.

Title: Must getBill track SaaS subscriptions and how many seats are used?
Why it matters: Unused SaaS seats are a common waste.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No.

Title: Where do SaaS costs come from?
Why it matters: Each source needs its own reader.
Examples of possible answers: Vendor invoices. A SaaS management tool. Corporate card statements.

Title: Must getBill report the carbon emissions of cloud usage?
Why it matters: Emissions reports need the providers' carbon data.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, for customers. Yes, for FPT only. No.

Title: Which providers' carbon data must be included?
Why it matters: Each provider publishes carbon data in its own way.
Examples of possible answers: AWS. Azure. Google Cloud.

Title: Who uses the emissions reports, and for what?
Why it matters: The use decides the detail and the timing.
Examples of possible answers: Annual sustainability reports. Customer requests.

Title: Which cloud cost policies exist today?
Why it matters: getBill may need to check them.
Examples of possible answers: Required tags. Approved Regions. Approved server types. Spending limits.

Title: Must getBill report how well each policy is followed?
Why it matters: The report shows where the policies fail.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No.

Title: Must new spending above a set amount be approved before it starts?
Why it matters: Approval stops surprises but slows teams down.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, above a monthly amount. No.

Title: How often should cost reviews take place, and who attends them?
Why it matters: Regular reviews keep costs in view.
Examples of possible answers: Monthly with each team. Quarterly with executives.

Title: Which FinOps maturity level does FPT aim to reach?
Why it matters: The target sets how much process getBill must support.
Examples of possible answers: Crawl. Walk. Run.

Title: Must any spending limits stop or slow usage automatically?
Why it matters: Hard limits protect budgets but can break services.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, for test accounts. No.

Title: How are new customers added today?
Why it matters: getBill should make this faster.
Examples of possible answers: By email and spreadsheets. Through a request form.

Title: How long may it take to add a new customer?
Why it matters: It sets how much must be automated.
Examples of possible answers: Less than a day. Less than a week.

Title: Which details must be collected for each new customer?
Why it matters: Missing details delay the first bill.
Examples of possible answers: Billing contacts. Accounts. Pricing rules. Currency.

Title: Must customers be able to add their own billing sources?
Why it matters: Self-service saves FPT staff time.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No, FPT staff add them.

Title: What should a customer's first bill cover when it starts partway through a month?
Why it matters: A partial month needs a clear rule.
Examples of possible answers: Only the days from the start date. The whole month.

Title: What happens to a customer's data when it leaves?
Why it matters: A leaving customer may need its data returned or deleted.
Examples of possible answers: Returned, then deleted. Kept for the retention period.

Title: What happens when an account moves from one customer or team to another?
Why it matters: A move splits one account's costs between two owners.
Examples of possible answers: Costs follow the account from the day of the move. The whole month goes to the new owner.

Title: How many customers will getBill serve now, and in two years?
Why it matters: The number of customers decides the design and the cost.
Examples of possible answers: Ten. One hundred. One thousand.

Title: When a customer starts buying AWS through FPT, do its existing AWS accounts move into FPT's AWS organization?
Why it matters: Moving accounts changes who receives AWS's bill and needs a clear switch-over date.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, the existing accounts move. New accounts are created. Both.

Title: When a customer stops buying AWS through FPT, how are its accounts handed back?
Why it matters: Removing accounts from FPT's organization ends FPT's billing and must match the final bill.
Examples of possible answers: Accounts leave on the last day of the month. Accounts leave immediately.

Title: How sensitive is billing data, and how is it classified?
Why it matters: The classification decides the security controls.
Examples of possible answers: Confidential. Internal.

Title: Which laws, contracts or policies apply to the data?
Why it matters: They limit where the data goes and who may see it.
Examples of possible answers: Customer contracts. Vietnam's personal data protection decree. GDPR.

Title: Which security framework must getBill meet?
Why it matters: The framework sets the controls and the documents.
Examples of possible answers: NIST SP 800-53 Moderate. ISO 27001. SOC 2. None.

Title: Are any customers government organizations?
Why it matters: Government customers bring their own security rules.
Examples of possible answers: No. U.S. federal agencies. State or local governments.

Title: Is any billing data Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI)?
Why it matters: CUI must be protected under NIST SP 800-171.
Examples of possible answers: No. Yes. Not known.

Title: Will getBill or any customer need a government cloud?
Why it matters: Government clouds have their own accounts, sign-in and rules.
Examples of possible answers: No. AWS GovCloud (US). Azure Government.

Title: Must the encryption use cryptographic modules validated under FIPS 140?
Why it matters: Many government contracts require it.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No.

Title: Who must control the encryption keys?
Why it matters: Keys that a customer controls need extra permissions for every reader.
Examples of possible answers: The cloud provider. FPT. Each customer.

Title: In which countries or Regions must billing data stay?
Why it matters: Data residency rules limit where data can be stored.
Examples of possible answers: The United States. Vietnam. Anywhere.

Title: May billing data from Azure and Google Cloud be copied into AWS?
Why it matters: Some rules forbid moving data from one provider to another.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No.

Title: Must each customer's data be stored apart from other customers' data?
Why it matters: Separate storage adds cost and setup work.
Examples of possible answers: Shared storage with strict access rules. A separate account for some customers. A separate account for every customer.

Title: Are there limits on who may see the data, or on where they work?
Why it matters: Some contracts allow only certain people or countries.
Examples of possible answers: Only U.S. persons. Only FPT staff.

Title: May billing data be copied to a person's computer?
Why it matters: Copies on laptops can leak.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. Only to company-managed computers. No.

Title: Which security documents must come with getBill for customers or auditors?
Why it matters: Buyers often ask for proof of secure development.
Examples of possible answers: A system security plan. Penetration test results. A software bill of materials.

Title: Must reports and the portal meet accessibility rules?
Why it matters: Section 508 applies to software used by U.S. federal agencies.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, Section 508. Yes, WCAG 2.1 level AA. No.

Title: Must getBill's totals match each provider's invoice?
Why it matters: Finance checks the bills against the invoice.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, to the cent. Within a stated tolerance. No.

Title: When is a month final?
Why it matters: Reporting before a provider closes a month gives numbers that change later.
Examples of possible answers: When the provider issues the invoice. A set number of days after the month ends.

Title: What should happen when a provider changes a month after it was billed?
Why it matters: Providers restate months after credits or refunds.
Examples of possible answers: Issue a corrected bill. Adjust the next month's bill. Ignore small changes.

Title: What should happen when billing data is late or missing on the deadline?
Why it matters: Customers are waiting for the bill.
Examples of possible answers: Wait and alert. Issue an estimated bill. Bill without that source.

Title: Which checks must pass before a bill is released?
Why it matters: Checks catch errors before customers see them.
Examples of possible answers: Totals match the invoice. No unassigned costs. Large changes reviewed.

Title: Who must be told when a check fails, and how quickly?
Why it matters: A failure that nobody sees means a late or wrong bill.
Examples of possible answers: The operations team within an hour. The product owner the next day.

Title: When a month is processed again, should the earlier results be replaced or kept as a version?
Why it matters: Earlier versions show what recipients saw on each date.
Examples of possible answers: Keep every version. Replace them.

Title: How long must raw billing data be kept?
Why it matters: Tax, audit and contract rules set minimum periods.
Examples of possible answers: 13 months. Seven years. Ten years.

Title: How long must issued bills be kept?
Why it matters: Bills are financial records.
Examples of possible answers: Seven years. Ten years.

Title: How long must audit records of who did what be kept?
Why it matters: Investigations need old records.
Examples of possible answers: One year. Seven years.

Title: Must issued bills be impossible to change or delete?
Why it matters: Auditors need proof that records were not altered.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No.

Title: How quickly must records be produced for an auditor?
Why it matters: Some audits have short deadlines.
Examples of possible answers: Within a day. Within a week.

Title: Who approves deleting data after its retention period ends?
Why it matters: A deletion must not break a legal hold.
Examples of possible answers: It happens automatically. Finance approves. Legal approves.

Title: Which accounting system must receive billing data?
Why it matters: Each system needs its own format or connection.
Examples of possible answers: SAP. Oracle NetSuite. QuickBooks. None.

Title: Which ticket system should getBill send work to?
Why it matters: Teams act on tickets in their own tools.
Examples of possible answers: Jira. ServiceNow. None.

Title: Which chat tools should getBill send messages to?
Why it matters: Alerts in chat get faster responses.
Examples of possible answers: Microsoft Teams. Slack. None.

Title: Must getBill read resource owners from a configuration management database?
Why it matters: A configuration management database can tell getBill who owns each resource.
Examples of possible answers: ServiceNow. None.

Title: Must other systems be able to read getBill's data through an API?
Why it matters: An API lets other tools reuse the data.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. No.

Title: Must getBill send its data to a company data warehouse?
Why it matters: A data warehouse lets other teams combine cost data with other data.
Examples of possible answers: Snowflake. Amazon Redshift. None.

Title: Who owns and supports getBill day to day?
Why it matters: Someone must fix it when it fails.
Examples of possible answers: The cloud team. A dedicated FinOps engineering team.

Title: During which hours must support be available?
Why it matters: Support hours decide the staffing.
Examples of possible answers: Business hours in Vietnam. Around the clock.

Title: How much downtime is acceptable for the portal and dashboards?
Why it matters: The availability target decides the design and its cost.
Examples of possible answers: 99.9% available. 99% available. Best effort.

Title: How quickly must getBill recover after a failure on a billing day?
Why it matters: The recovery time decides backups and failover.
Examples of possible answers: Within four hours. Within one day.

Title: How much data may be lost after a failure?
Why it matters: It decides how often data is backed up.
Examples of possible answers: None. One day. One week.

Title: How large is a month's billing data today, and how fast is it growing?
Why it matters: Size decides storage and processing costs.
Examples of possible answers: A few gigabytes. Hundreds of gigabytes. Doubling each year.

Title: How must changes to getBill be tested and approved before release?
Why it matters: Untested changes can corrupt bills.
Examples of possible answers: Automatic tests and a review. A test environment first.

Title: Which separate environments are needed?
Why it matters: Separate environments keep test changes away from real bills.
Examples of possible answers: Development, test and production. Production only.

Title: Which manual steps are used today to produce bills and reports?
Why it matters: Each step must be rebuilt in getBill.
Examples of possible answers: Exporting data. Copying it into Excel. Running macros. Emailing files.

Title: Which Excel workbooks and VBA macros are used today?
Why it matters: Each one must be listed before it can be replaced.
Examples of possible answers: One workbook for each customer. A shared pricing workbook.

Title: Who maintains each workbook and macro?
Why it matters: The people who maintain them know the hidden rules.
Examples of possible answers: A finance analyst. The cloud team.

Title: How long should getBill and the old process run side by side?
Why it matters: Running both shows whether getBill's results match.
Examples of possible answers: One month. Two months. Until finance approves.

Title: What must match before the old process stops?
Why it matters: A clear test prevents surprises for customers.
Examples of possible answers: Every customer's total, to the cent. Totals within 1%.

Title: Which customers still need Excel files, and until when?
Why it matters: It decides how long Excel output must be kept.
Examples of possible answers: None. Some, until their contracts renew.

Title: Which past bills must be loaded into getBill?
Why it matters: Customers may ask about old bills.
Examples of possible answers: None. The last 12 months.
